title: Tilda and the Stubborn Cloud-Sheep
markdown:
The wind in the northern ranges had a bite that could make an icicle shiver. Stone towers clung to the mountainsides like grumpy barnacles. Below, ravines held a swirling sea of mist so pearly you might swear it had been spun from moonlight. In one of those sky-high towers, perched so high it tickled the bellies of the clouds, lived Witch Tilda.

Tilda was not the cackling, broomstick-zooming sort. Her magic was practical. She could mend a leaky cauldron with a whisper, and coax stubborn mountain herbs to sprout with a hum that vibrated through her sensible boots. Her familiar, Pipkin, was a hedgehog of remarkable intelligence and an even more remarkable talent for sniffing out good ideas. His quills were the warm colour of autumn leaves. His obsidian eyes missed nothing. He believed Tilda’s quiet competence was the finest magic in the known lands, and he was not a hedgehog given to exaggeration.

This year Crag’s Edge, a mist-swaddled village in a scenic valley, would hold the annual Sparkle & Shine Festival. Every witch and wizard from miles around was expected to present a dazzling, flamboyant display. Tilda felt a rumble of discontent, right in her sensible boots.

“All this flashy magic is well and good for fireworks, Pipkin,” she said one crisp morning, voice as warm as a hearth. “But what about the everyday wonders? A truly sensible solution to a vexing problem that crops up when you least expect it?”

Pipkin twitched his nose. “Sensible is good, Tilda. Very, very good.”

“Exactly. I am going to prove that a simple, clever idea is worth more than any puff of smoke. I am entering the Most Ingenious Problem Solver category.”

She polished her best pair of sensible gardening shears and considered the matter settled.

The morning of the festival dawned bright and sharp as a newly honed icicle. Tilda had Pipkin in her pocket and the shears in her satchel when a frantic knocking rattled the cauldrons.

Agnes, from the next ridge over, stood on the step. Agnes’s magic tended toward ruffles, a startlingly loud cackle, and flamboyant pronouncements. Today the ruffles were dishevelled, and the cackle had gone missing.

“Tilda! You simply must help me. It’s Nimbus. He’s being positively heroic!”

Nimbus was Agnes’s prize: a cloud-sheep so impossibly fluffy and white you could get lost in him, like a gentle airy hug. Usually he floated beside her like a miniature cumulus that had sprouted four little cloud-legs. Today he had made a solemn decision. He would go absolutely nowhere. He was planted on Agnes’s doorstep, cloud-legs dug into the rocky path as if they were roots. No coaxing, no gentlest magic, would budge him. He was, in a word, heroically stubborn.

“The competition starts in less than an hour,” Agnes wrung her hands. “Nimbus was supposed to be my grand finale. A demonstration of ethereal lightness. How can I show that if he will not move?”

Tilda sighed, a tiny puff of almost invisible smoke. “Heroically stubborn, you say.” A whisper and a hum would not quite solve that. She glanced at Pipkin. Pipkin glanced back, a whole universe of quiet support in two dark eyes. “If he’s being heroically stubborn, Agnes, perhaps he needs a heroically sensible solution.”

They trooped down the winding path. Nimbus waited: a magnificent fluffy monument to defiance, utterly immovable.

Agnes tried a shimmering charm designed to make small objects float. Nimbus remained earthbound. She whispered persuasions strong enough to make a reluctant gnome tap-dance. Nimbus blinked his large sheepy eyes, unmoved. Tilda, ever the pragmatist, tried a little nudge with the polished shears. Nimbus seemed to gain weight, sinking deeper into the rock. Pipkin nudged the woolly ankles with a determined snout. Nimbus fluffed up like a startled dandelion.

Villagers were already gathering. Crystal trees hummed. Fountains spouted rainbow water. Miniature dragons breathed harmless glittering sparks. The air buzzed with ozone and anticipation. Tilda felt the familiar tug of quiet desperation. This was precisely the mule-headed silliness that grand magic often failed to fix.

“He’s not just stubborn,” Agnes whimpered. “He’s philosophically stubborn. He has made up his mind that he isn’t going anywhere.”

Tilda knelt beside Nimbus, ignoring the admiring glances and the occasional pitying tut. She was not thinking about grand magic. She was thinking about Pipkin, and their own tower, and the special mosses that grew only on the north side of rocks, smelling of rain and cool damp earth after a long absence.

She murmured clicks and soft whistles. Pipkin’s ears perked. He scampered off behind Agnes’s tower like a furry shadow.

“What on earth are you doing?” Agnes asked. “A giant sheep-herding dog?”

“Nothing so dramatic. A bit of inspiration. A rather specific kind.”

Pipkin returned with a small leafy clump of that north-side moss, still damp, clinging to rough rock, smelling of the mountain’s hidden places. Tilda took it gently.

“Nimbus, my dear boy,” she said, holding the moss so the earthy scent drifted toward him. “You’re a cloud-sheep. You enjoy the things clouds and sky enjoy. But sometimes even the sky likes a good damp earthly smell. This moss grows only where the sun never quite reaches. Rare. And if I am not mistaken, very tasty for a discerning cloud-sheep.”

Nimbus, unmoved by dazzling charms, tilted his fluffy head. He took a tentative sniff. Ears twitched. Another, deeper sniff. Then, with a bleat that sounded remarkably like curiosity, he took a small hesitant step. Cloud-hooves thudded softly. He lowered his head and nibbled.

Tilda offered another piece. Another step. Another. He was moving — slowly, deliberately, but moving. She led him down the path toward the square, crumb by crumb. Pipkin trotted beside her, quills vibrating with a satisfaction only Tilda could hear. Villagers gasped, then broke into cheering. The sensible solution was actually working.

They reached the square as the final competition bell gathered itself to chime. Nimbus, no longer heroically stubborn but heroically engrossed in moss, ambled into his designated spot, looking surprisingly content and remarkably fluffy. Tilda, with a simple nod, presented her polished gardening shears.

The judges — a panel of particularly wise-looking mountain goats with impressively long beards — peered at the shears. Then at Tilda. Then at the happily munching Nimbus, who had by now finished the entire clump.

The shears took first prize for Most Ingenious Problem Solver. Not for their sharpness. For the idea behind them: that the best tool for a job is often the one you already possess, used with clever thought and a dash of understanding.

The festival went on. Tilda’s quiet victory was celebrated not with thunderous applause but with steaming mugs of spiced berry cider and plates of honey cakes. Witches who had dazzled with illusions and levitation gathered round to ask how to prune a grumpy apple tree, or how to encourage shy moon-blossoms. Nimbus, having enjoyed his adventure and the rare moss, looked far less inclined toward heroic defiance. Agnes’s ruffles recovered a little of their pride.

As silvery moonlight spilled over the high rope bridge that connected Crag’s Edge to the world beyond, Tilda sat with Pipkin in her pocket, shears across her knees, and watched Nimbus float — actually float — a few inches above the square, as if stubbornness, once fed, had remembered it could also be light.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
